analysis.one_liner: Pays landowners when endangered species protections cut their property's value by half or more.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote and drew no cosponsors, dying quietly in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the Endangered Species Act so that whenever a federal agency's action to protect a listed species cuts the value of any portion of private land by 50 percent or more, the agency must either pay the owner for that loss or buy the land outright at its pre-restriction value — appraised as if no endangered species were present. Owners who sued and won would also collect attorney's fees and appraisal costs from the agency's own budget. It would have created a Species Conservation Fund for voluntary land acquisition and capped required habitat mitigation so it could not exceed the footprint or cost of the damaging activity.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of large or valuable land restricted to protect endangered species — developers, timber and mining interests, and agricultural landholders — would gain a new federal entitlement to cash or buyouts, with fees and costs covered on top. They could take claims to binding arbitration or court, and prevailing owners recover attorney's fees and appraisal costs from the agency [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Any federal agency action that diminishes the value of a portion of private property by 50 percent or more triggers a duty to compensate the owner or, at the owner's option, buy that portion at its pre-diminution fair market value — appraised without regard to the presence or use of an endangered species [S2][S3].

Owners could bypass negotiation after 180 days and elect binding arbitration or a civil action, and prevailing owners would recover just compensation with compounded interest, reasonable attorney's fees, and litigation and appraisal costs [S2][S3].

The bill would cap mitigation requirements so the government could not require habitat offsets larger in area or cost than the activity causing the harm, limiting the conservation conditions placed on development [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through the annual appropriations of the agencies whose conservation actions trigger claims, and the public, which would see habitat protections become far more expensive for agencies to impose — likely deterring some protections altogether [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Compensation and buyout payments would come out of the responsible agency's own annual appropriations, meaning every dollar paid to landowners is a dollar not spent on that agency's conservation work [S3].

Requiring buyouts at values appraised 'without regard to the presence on the property of an endangered or threatened species' would inflate the price taxpayers pay and give agencies a strong financial reason to avoid listing actions or habitat protections in the first place, weakening species recovery [S2][S3].

The proposed cap on mitigation — allowing offsets no larger in area than the impacted land and costing no more than fencing — would limit the standard tool agencies use to offset habitat loss, drawing opposition from conservationists [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers genuine security to a small set of owners whose property value is sharply cut by species protections, and it pairs the compensation mandate with a conservation land fund. But the costs run wide and deep: agencies paying out of their own budgets would have every incentive to take fewer actions to protect habitat, and the mitigation cap would shrink offsets for the damage that does occur. The trade is a large, open-ended liability on taxpayers and weaker species protection in exchange for a compensation right for a concentrated group of large landholders.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Natural Resources Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no vote, and not a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. William M. Thomas introduced the bill on September 11, 1998, near the end of the 105th Congress, and it was referred to the House Committee on Resources [S1][S5].
The committee took no further action on the bill before that Congress ended on January 3, 1999, so it never reached the House floor [S5].
No member joined as a cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Endangered species protections and the agencies that enforce them are better off, since no compensation mandate was added; large landowners lose the chance at a new federal payout stream.

industries.industry: Real estate developers and large landholders
industries.note: The bill would create a federal right to compensation or buyouts when species protections cut property value by 50 percent or more, appraised as if no endangered species existed. Their gain is paid by taxpayers and comes at the cost of weaker habitat protection on private land.

These land-heavy industries face the most frequent ESA use restrictions on timber harvest, minerals, grazing, and water rights — all explicitly covered by the bill's broad definition of property. The mitigation cap would also limit the offsets they can be required to provide.

industries.industry: Endangered species conservation programs (federal and nonprofit land acquisition)
industries.note: The bill would establish a Species Conservation Fund for habitat acquisition on private land, but it depends on annual appropriations and would sit alongside a compensation regime that discourages agencies from acting to protect habitat at all.
